26.explanation_en:
The term "Bully" is historically and traditionally used in
Field Hockey as a method to restart play after an in-
jury or stoppage where neither team was at fault.
Important Facts:
➤ In Field Hockey, a "Bully" involves two opposing
players tapping the ground and each other's sticks alter-
nately before playing the ball.
➤ Modern field hockey rules have replaced the bully in
most situations with a free hit or bully restarts un-
der specific circumstances.
➤ Other well-known terms associated with hockey in-
clude penalty corner, scoop, dribble, green
card, and roll-in.
➤ The international governing body for the sport is the
International Hockey Federation (FIH).
➤ Field Hockey is played with a stick and a hard com-
posite ball between two teams of 11 players each.

In Tennis, a double fault occurs when a server
misses both the first and second serves into the legal
service box, resulting in the loss of that point.
Important Facts:
➤ A player serving in tennis is permitted two attempts;
failing both sequentially constitutes a double fault.
➤ Tennis scoring follows the sequence: 15, 30, 40,
and game; tied at 40-40 is referred to as Deuce.
➤ The four Grand Slam tournaments in tennis are the
Australian Open, French Open (Roland
Garros), Wimbledon, and US Open.
➤ Other common terms in tennis include ace, let,
baseline, love, volley, and smash.
➤ The governing body of global tennis is the
International Tennis Federation (ITF).

medal at the Asian Games?

Kamaljeet Sandhu became the first Indian woman
athlete to win a gold medal at the Asian Games by win-
ning the 400m race at the 1970 Bangkok Asian
Games.
Important Facts:
➤ Kamaljeet Sandhu clocked 57.3 seconds to win
the gold medal in the 400-metre sprint at Bangkok in
1970.
➤ She was conferred the prestigious Padma Shri
award in 1971 in recognition of her landmark athletic
achievement.
➤ M.D. Valsamma was the second Indian woman to
win an individual Asian Games gold (400m hurdles in
1982 New Delhi).
➤ P.T. Usha won multiple gold medals in the 1986
Seoul Asian Games.
➤ The Asian Games are organized every four years by
the Olympic Council of Asia (OCA).

30.question_text_en:
Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (QUAD) was originally
proposed in which year?
30.question_text_hi:
Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (QUAD) was originally
proposed in which year?
30.explanation_en:
The idea of the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue
(QUAD) was first initiated and proposed in 2007 by the
then Prime Minister of Japan, Shinzo Abe. It brings to-
gether four nations: India, the United States,
Japan, and Australia.
Important Facts:
➤ The concept of QUAD originated following coopera-
tion during the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami.
➤ Former Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe for-
mally pitched the idea in 2007.
➤ After remaining dormant for several years, the group
was revived in November 2017.
➤ The four member nations are India, the USA,
Australia, and Japan.
➤ The member states regularly participate in the joint
multilateral maritime exercise called Exercise
Malabar.

informs our understanding of economic organization in the
Indus Valley Civilization?

Which of the following interpretations best explains
how the evidence of craft materials and transport models
informs our understanding of economic organization in the
Indus Valley Civilization?

options.text_en: Local clay shows little long-distance trade.
options.text_hi: Local clay shows little long-distance trade.

options.text_en: External materials and routes show integrated exchange.
options.text_hi: External materials and routes show integrated exchange.

options.text_hi: Bullock cart models prove only overland trade.

options.text_en: River/coastal routes mean crafts centralized near water.
options.text_hi: River/coastal routes mean crafts centralized near water.

31.explanation_en:
The presence of raw materials sourced from distant re-
gions (e.g., lapis lazuli, carnelian, copper) alongside ter-
racotta transport models demonstrates an advanced, in-
tegrated regional and inter-regional exchange
network in Harappan society.
Important Facts:
➤ Harappans obtained copper from the Khetri mines
of Rajasthan and tin possibly from Afghanistan.

➤ Lapis lazuli, a prized blue stone, was procured
from Shortughai in northeastern Afghanistan.
➤ Carnelian was sourced primarily from Bharuch in
Gujarat, while steatite came from south Rajasthan and
north Gujarat.
➤ Archaeological finds of terracotta toy carts and
seal depictions of boats reveal both overland and
maritime/riverine trade.
➤ Maritime trade with Mesopotamia is corroborated
by Mesopotamian texts referring to trade with Meluhha
(Indus region).

32.question_text_en:
The 'Dahsala System' of land revenue, introduced by
Raja Todar Mal, was based on the average of which of the
following?
32.question_text_hi:
The 'Dahsala System' of land revenue, introduced by
Raja Todar Mal, was based on the average of which of the
following?
32.explanation_en:
The Ain-i-Dahsala (Dahsala System) was intro-
duced in 1580 during Akbar's reign by finance minister
Raja Todar Mal, calculating tax based on the average
agricultural yield and prices of the last ten years
(1570–1580).
Important Facts:
➤ The Dahsala system was promulgated in 1580 CE
under the Mughal Emperor Akbar.
➤ It was devised by Akbar's finance minister Raja
Todar Mal, who was one of the Navaratnas.
➤ Land revenue was assessed as one-third (1/3rd)
of the average produce of the previous ten years.
➤ Under this system, agricultural lands were classified
into four categories: Polaj, Parauti, Chachar, and
Banjar.
➤ It provided stability to cultivators by avoiding yearly
arbitrariness in revenue calculation.

➤ Land revenue was assessed as one-third (1/3rd)
of the average produce of the previous ten years.

into four categories: Polaj, Parauti, Chachar, and
Banjar.
➤ It provided stability to cultivators by avoiding yearly
arbitrariness in revenue calculation.

33.explanation_en:
The semantic evolution of the term 'Hindu'—from an Old
Persian geographical descriptor for people living beyond
the Indus (Sindhu) River to a distinct religious identifier—
exemplifies how social categories evolve and ac-
quire new meanings over historical periods.
Important Facts:
➤ The word 'Hindu' derives from the Sanskrit root
Sindhu, referring to the Indus River system.
➤ In ancient Achaemenid Persian inscriptions (e.g.,
Darius I at Persepolis/Naqsh-e-Rustam), Hiduš was
employed purely as a geographic designation.
➤ The Greeks modified the term to Indos, from which
the European term India originated.
➤ In Arabic and Persian medieval texts, the term Al-
Hind denoted the geographic territory and its inhabi-
tants.
➤ Only in late medieval and colonial periods did the
term gradually solidify into a cohesive religious identity.

34.question_text_en:
Who was the tribal revolutionary leader responsible
for leading the Rampa Rebellion of 1922 against the
British Forest Acts?
34.question_text_hi:
Who was the tribal revolutionary leader responsible
for leading the Rampa Rebellion of 1922 against the
British Forest Acts?
34.explanation_en:
Alluri Sitarama Raju led the historic Rampa
Rebellion (Manyam Rebellion) of 1922–1924 in
the Godavari agency area against oppressive British
colonial forest laws.
Important Facts:
➤ The Rampa Rebellion occurred between 1922
and 1924 in the present-day Andhra Pradesh region.
➤ Alluri Sitarama Raju organized local Adivasis against
the restrictive Madras Forest Act, 1882, which
banned their traditional Podu (shifting) cultivation.
➤ He effectively used guerrilla warfare tactics
against the colonial police and armed forces.
➤ He was affectionately given the title Manyam
Veerudu (Hero of the Jungles) by the local people.
➤ Raju was captured and executed by the British forces
in May 1924.

35.question_text_en:
Which term refers to the excess of government
expenditure over its receipts excluding borrowings?
35.question_text_hi:
Which term refers to the excess of government
expenditure over its receipts excluding borrowings?
35.explanation_en:
Fiscal deficit is defined as the difference between to-
tal government expenditure and total receipts, excluding
non-debt borrowings.
Important Facts:
➤ The formula for Fiscal Deficit is: Total
Expenditure − (Total Receipts excluding
Borrowings).
➤ It reflects the total borrowing requirement of the gov-
ernment from all sources during a financial year.
➤ Revenue Deficit refers specifically to the excess
of revenue expenditure over revenue receipts.
➤ Primary Deficit is calculated as Fiscal Deficit
minus Interest Payments.
➤ The FRBM Act, 2003 was enacted in India to insti-
tutionalize fiscal discipline and reduce deficits.

36.question_text_en:
Fill in the blank: Payments made by the government
without any goods or services in return are called
________ payments.
36.question_text_hi:
Fill in the blank: Payments made by the government
without any goods or services in return are called
________ payments.
36.explanation_en:
Transfer payments are one-way payments made by
the government to individuals or entities without receiv-
ing any direct productive good or service in return.
Important Facts:
➤ Common examples of transfer payments include old-
age pensions, unemployment allowances, and
student scholarships.
➤ Transfer payments are not included in the calcula-
tion of National Income (GDP) because they do not re-
flect current production.
➤ Unlike factor payments (wages, interest, rent), trans-
fer payments are unilateral transactions.
➤ In macroeconomics, they serve as redistribution
mechanisms to reduce economic inequality.
➤ Social security benefits are categorized as public
transfer payments.

growth rate for the Sixth Five-Year Plan?

➤ Major poverty alleviation programmes like the
Integrated Rural Development Programme
(IRDP) and TRYSEM were emphasized.
➤ The NABARD (National Bank for Agriculture and
Rural Development) was established during this plan in
1982.
➤ The plan marked the beginning of economic liberal-
ization in the Indian economy.

38.question_text_en:
Fill in the blank: The government identifies certain
high-performing PSUs and grants them greater autonomy
by giving them the status of 'Navratna' or '________'.
38.question_text_hi:
Fill in the blank: The government identifies certain
high-performing PSUs and grants them greater autonomy
by giving them the status of 'Navratna' or '________'.
38.explanation_en:
The Government of India categorizes profitable Central
Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) into Maharatna,
Navratna, and Miniratna (Category-I and Category-
II) to confer operational and financial autonomy.
Important Facts:
➤ The Navratna and Miniratna schemes were first
introduced by the Government of India in 1997.
➤ In 2009, the government introduced an even higher
category known as Maharatna for mega-enterprises.
➤ Miniratna CPSEs are sub-divided into two groups:
Category-I and Category-II, based on profitability
and net worth.
➤ These statuses allow PSU boards to incur capital ex-
penditures without prior government approval up to de-
fined monetary ceilings.
➤ The categorization is administered by the
Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) under
the Ministry of Finance.

39.question_text_en:
Which of the following punishments is newly
introduced in Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023?
39.question_text_hi:
Which of the following punishments is newly
introduced in Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023?
39.explanation_en:
Community service has been introduced as a new
form of punishment for petty offences under Section 4 of
the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS).
Important Facts:
➤ Section 4 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita,
2023 explicitly adds Community service to the list
of recognized punishments.
➤ It is intended for minor and petty offences like small
thefts, defamation, or public misconduct to encourage
reformative justice.
➤ The BNS, 2023 replaced the colonial-era Indian
Penal Code (IPC) of 1860.
➤ Other traditional punishments retained include death,
imprisonment for life, imprisonment (rigorous/simple),
forfeiture of property, and fine.
➤ The new criminal laws came into legal enforcement
across India on 1 July 2024.

40.question_text_en:
Under Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS),
which of the following best reflects the shift in approach
regarding FIR registration?
40.question_text_hi:
Under Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS),
which of the following best reflects the shift in approach
regarding FIR registration?

options.text_en: An FIR can be registered only within jurisdiction.
options.text_hi: An FIR can be registered only within jurisdiction.

options.text_en: A preliminary inquiry is mandatory in all cases.
options.text_hi: A preliminary inquiry is mandatory in all cases.

options.text_en: Police have absolute discretion to refuse FIRs.
options.text_hi: Police have absolute discretion to refuse FIRs.

options.text_en: E-FIR and zero FIR concepts are strengthened.
options.text_hi: E-FIR and zero FIR concepts are strengthened.

40.explanation_en:
Under Section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik
Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), provisions for
registering an e-FIR (electronic communication) and for-
mal statutory recognition of Zero FIR (irrespective of
jurisdiction) have been explicitly strengthened.
Important Facts:
➤ The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita,
2023 (BNSS) replaced the colonial-era Code of
Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC).
➤ Section 173 of BNSS allows information about cog-
nizable offences to be given electronically (e-FIR).
➤ It also mandates that an FIR can be registered at any
police station regardless of jurisdiction (Zero FIR), to
be transferred later.
➤ For e-FIRs, the informant must sign the formal docu-
ment within three days of submission.
➤ The new criminal procedural code came into force
across India on 1 July 2024.

41.question_text_en:
Which earthquake waves travel fastest through the
Earth?
41.question_text_hi:
Which earthquake waves travel fastest through the
Earth?
41.explanation_en:
Primary waves (P-waves) are longitudinal compres-
sional waves and are the fastest seismic waves, travel-
ing through the Earth and arriving first at seismograph
stations.
Important Facts:
➤ P-waves travel at velocities between 5 to 8 km/s
in the Earth's crust, which is faster than S-waves and
surface waves.
➤ P-waves can propagate through all three mediums:
solids, liquids, and gases.
➤ They are longitudinal waves, meaning particle
motion is parallel to the direction of wave propagation.
➤ Secondary waves (S-waves) are slower trans-
verse waves and can travel only through solids.
➤
Surface waves (Rayleigh and Love waves)
are the slowest but typically cause the greatest structural
damage.

membrane space of the mitochondria into the cy-
tosol, triggering caspase activation.

of the cell" because they synthesize ATP via cellular
respiration.

membrane permeabilization causes the release of cy-
tochrome c.

Apaf-1 to form the apoptosome, which activates ini-
tiator caspases.
➤ Mitochondria possess their own double-stranded cir-
cular DNA and 70S ribosomes.
➤ The inner mitochondrial membrane contains folds
known as cristae to increase surface area.

LVM3 rocket?
44.question_text_hi:
Which mission preceded the LVM3-M5 flight of the
LVM3 rocket?

LVM3-M4 rocket flight on 14 July 2023, making it the
immediate predecessor to the LVM3-M5 operational
launch vehicle flight.

designated as the LVM3-M4 mission.

previously designated as the GSLV Mk III.
➤ LVM3 is a three-stage launch vehicle with two solid
strap-on motors (S200), a liquid core stage (L110), and
a cryogenic upper stage (C25).
➤ Chandrayaan-3 achieved a historic soft landing on
the south polar region of the Moon on 23 August
2023.
➤ Aditya-L1 was launched using the PSLV-C57
rocket, not an LVM3 vehicle.

46.question_text_en:
What is the primary goal of geoengineering
interventions?
46.question_text_hi:
What is the primary goal of geoengineering
interventions?
46.explanation_en:
The primary goal of climate geoengineering
(specifically Carbon Dioxide Removal techniques) is to
deliberately mitigate global warming by removing
greenhouse gases from the atmosphere or reflecting
solar radiation.
Important Facts:
➤ Geoengineering interventions are broadly catego-
rized into Solar Radiation Management (SRM)
and Carbon Dioxide Removal (CDR).
➤ Carbon Dioxide Removal (CDR) technologies
capture and sequester carbon dioxide directly from the
atmosphere.
➤ Examples of CDR include direct air capture
(DAC), afforestation, and ocean fertilization.
➤ The ultimate objective of geoengineering is to counter
anthropogenic climate change and lower planetary
heating.
➤ These technologies are studied extensively under the
Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change
(IPCC) frameworks.

Development Programme (UNDP) as part of its
Human Development Report.

➤ The HDI was devised and introduced in 1990 by
Pakistani economist Mahbub ul Haq and Indian econ-
omist Amartya Sen.

expectancy, education (mean and expected
years of schooling), and gross national income
(GNI) per capita.
➤ The report is published annually under the aegis of
the United Nations Development Programme
(UNDP).
➤ The HDI value ranges on a scale between 0 and 1,

with higher values representing greater human develop-
ment.
➤ The UNDP headquarters is located in New York
City, USA.

26.question_text_en: What is the "Cant" in Kabaddi?
26.question_text_hi: What is the "Cant" in Kabaddi?
26.explanation_en:
In Kabaddi, the "Cant" refers to the continuous and
clear audible chanting of the approved word "kabaddi"
in a single unbroken breath by the raider while in the
opponent's court.
Important Facts:
➤ A raider must begin the cant before entering the
opponent's court and sustain it until returning safely to
their home half.

➤ If the raider loses or breaks the cant while inside the
opponent's territory, they are declared out, and the de-
fending team is awarded a point.
➤ Standard match raid durations are capped at a maxi-
mum of 30 seconds.
➤ Kabaddi was introduced as a regular medal sport at
the Asian Games in 1990 (Beijing).
➤ The International Kabaddi Federation (IKF) is the
apex international governing body for the sport.

28.question_text_en:
Which instrument produces sound without being
continuously struck by the player?
28.question_text_hi:
Which instrument produces sound without being
continuously struck by the player?
28.explanation_en:
A Damaru produces sound via knotted cords or beads
that strike its two drumheads alternately as the player
twists their wrist back and forth, rather than being struck
directly by hands or sticks.
Important Facts:
➤ The Damaru is a small, hourglass-shaped membra-
nophone associated iconographically with Lord Shiva
in Indian tradition.
➤ Unlike direct-struck drums like the mridangam, tavil,
or nagara, the sound is generated by the swinging mo-
mentum of knotted strings.
➤ In classical Indian classification of musical instru-
ments (*Natya Shastra*), percussion instruments are
categorized as Avanaddha Vadya.
➤ The Mridangam and Tavil are classical South
Indian percussion instruments struck manually with
hands or a combination of hand and stick.
➤ The Nagara is a large kettle-drum commonly beaten

with two curved wooden beaters in folk and temple
traditions.

29.question_text_en:
Which dance form integrates "vachika abhinaya"
(spoken word) along with expressive dance?
29.question_text_hi:
Which dance form integrates "vachika abhinaya"
(spoken word) along with expressive dance?
29.explanation_en:
Kuchipudi, originating from Andhra Pradesh, uniquely
incorporates vachika abhinaya (where performers
deliver dialogues and spoken lines alongside dance and
music).
Important Facts:
➤ Kuchipudi originated in the Kuchipudi village in
Krishna district of Andhra Pradesh.
➤ It was systematized and popularized in the 17th cen-
tury by the saint-poet Siddhendra Yogi.
➤ Unlike many classical forms focusing exclusively on
angika abhinaya, traditional Kuchipudi involves dance-

drama where actors speak and sing.
➤ A distinctive feature of Kuchipudi performance is
Tarangam, where dancers perform on the edges of a
brass plate.
➤ The performance traditionally begins with the invoca-
tion ritual known as the Purvaranga.

banization.

Census of India since 1872 and the 7th after
independence.

through the Bangkok Declaration.
➤ It initially began as BIST-EC (Bangladesh, India, Sri

leading to the present official name.
➤ The permanent secretariat of BIMSTEC is located in
Dhaka, Bangladesh.
➤ The member countries together account for roughly
22% of the global population.

33.question_text_en: The 'UDAN' scheme is aimed at:
33.question_text_hi: The 'UDAN' scheme is aimed at:
33.explanation_en:
The UDAN (*Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik*) scheme is an
initiative launched by the Ministry of Civil Aviation to en-
hance regional air connectivity and make air travel
affordable for common citizens.
Important Facts:
➤ The UDAN scheme was officially launched in
October 2016 under the National Civil Aviation Policy
(NCAP).
➤ The first UDAN flight was flagged off by Prime
Minister Narendra Modi on 27 April 2017, connecting
Shimla to Delhi.
➤ It provides financial incentives and Viability Gap
Funding (VGF) to airlines to operate flights on un-
served and underserved regional routes.
➤ Airfares under the scheme are capped for 50% of
seats at subsidized rates for fixed-wing aircraft flying dis-
tances up to 500 km or 1 hour.
➤ The Airports Authority of India (AAI) serves as the
designated implementing agency for the scheme.

34.question_text_en: The name "Earth" is derived from:
34.question_text_hi: The name "Earth" is derived from:
34.explanation_en:
Unlike all other planets in our solar system which are
named after Greek and Roman deities, the name
"Earth" originates from Old English (*eorþe*) and
Germanic words meaning "ground" or "soil".
Important Facts:
➤ The word traces back to Proto-Germanic *ertho*
and Old Saxon *ertha*.
➤ Earth is the only planet in the solar system not
named after a mythological Greco-Roman god or god-
dess.
➤ In Roman mythology, the goddess of Earth is known
as Terra Mater (or Tellus).
➤ In Greek mythology, the personification of Earth is
Gaia.
➤ Earth is the third planet from the Sun and the densest
planet in the solar system.

the Bodhi tree in Bodh Gaya, Bihar.

36.question_text_en:
Fill in the blank: The symbolic element described as
being placed "around the head" of Buddha and
Bodhisattva figures in the Gandhara School of Art is
________.
36.question_text_hi:
Fill in the blank: The symbolic element described as
being placed "around the head" of Buddha and
Bodhisattva figures in the Gandhara School of Art is
________.
36.explanation_en:
In the Greco-Buddhist Gandhara School of Art, a
prominent halo (prabhamandala) is sculpted around
the head of the Buddha and Bodhisattvas to represent
divine radiance and spiritual enlightenment.
Important Facts:
➤ Gandhara art developed primarily during the rule of
the Kushan Empire, flourishing under Emperor
Kanishka.
➤ It is characterized by heavy Greco-Roman
Hellenistic artistic influences merged with Buddhist
iconographic motifs.
➤ The halo was adopted from Hellenistic depictions of
Apollo and solar deities to signify supreme spiritual wis-
dom.
➤ Sculptures in Gandhara art were predominantly made
using grey sandstone and stucco.
➤ Other prominent stylistic features include wavy hair,
realistic anatomical drapery, and sharp facial features.

and persistent increase in the general price
level of goods and services in an economy over a pe-
riod of time.

Authority (NALSA) v. Union of India (2014), the
Supreme Court of India legally recognized transgender
persons as the 'third gender' and affirmed their fun-
damental rights under the Constitution.
Important Facts:
➤ The judgment was delivered by a bench comprising
Justice K.S. Radhakrishnan and Justice A.K.
Sikri in April 2014.
➤ The court affirmed that fundamental rights granted
under Articles 14, 15, 19, and 21 apply equally to
transgender individuals.
➤ It directed central and state governments to treat
transgender persons as socially and educationally
backward classes (SEBC) for reservations.
➤
Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018)
decriminalized consensual homosexual acts under
Section 377 of the IPC.
➤
K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017)
unanimously held the Right to Privacy to be a funda-
mental right under Article 21.

40.question_text_en:
Which organization is responsible for enforcing
criminal laws in India?
40.question_text_hi:
Which organization is responsible for enforcing
criminal laws in India?
40.explanation_en:
In India, the enforcement and administration of criminal
law fall under the mandate of the Police (investigation
and law enforcement) and the Judiciary (adjudication
and sentencing).
Important Facts:
➤ Under the Seventh Schedule of the Indian
Constitution, 'Police' and 'Public Order' are State
subjects under List II.
➤ Parliament possesses the power to enact and
amend substantive and procedural criminal laws such as
the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS).
➤ The Judiciary ensures due process, protects con-
stitutional safeguards, and issues penal sentences upon
trial conviction.
➤ The Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) /
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS)
governs criminal procedural enforcement in India.
➤ Law enforcement agencies investigate cognizable of-
fences under statutory mandates without prior judicial
warrants.

41.question_text_en:
What are the specialized receptors that detect the
sensation of taste called?
41.question_text_hi:
What are the specialized receptors that detect the
sensation of taste called?
41.explanation_en:
Sensory receptors that detect taste stimuli are known as
gustatory receptors, predominantly clustered within
taste buds on the tongue surface.
Important Facts:
➤ Humans recognize five primary taste modalities:
sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami.
➤ Receptors responsible for detecting the sense of
smell are known as olfactory receptors.
➤ Taste buds reside within elevated projections on the
tongue known as papillae (circumvallate, foliate, and
fungiform).
➤ Taste sensations are relayed to the central nervous
system via cranial nerves VII (Facial), IX
(Glossopharyngeal), and X (Vagus).
➤ Gustatory perception combines closely with olfactory
signals to create overall flavor perception in the brain.

tured detailed observations of active regions and a so-
lar flare kernel in the near-ultraviolet wavelength
range.

maiden solar observatory, Aditya-L1, launched on 2
September 2023.

Earth Lagrange point 1 (L1), roughly 1.5 million
km from Earth.

for Astronomy and Astrophysics (IUCAA) in Pune.
➤ The telescope records full-disk images of the Sun in
the 200 to 400 nm near-ultraviolet (NUV) spectrum.
➤ The observations help scientists study the dynamics
of the solar chromosphere, photosphere, and solar flare
eruptions.

indigenous satellite capacity

44.explanation_en:
Developing the indigenous PSLV granted India autono-
mous, self-reliant launch capabilities, substantially re-
ducing expensive reliance on foreign space
agencies while enabling independent deployment of
Earth observation, navigation, and scientific satellites.
Important Facts:
➤ The Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV) was devel-
oped by the Indian Space Research Organisation
(ISRO) and had its first successful flight in October
1994 (PSLV-D2).
➤ Regarded as the "Workhorse of ISRO", PSLV is
a versatile four-stage launch vehicle utilizing alternating
solid and liquid propulsion stages.
➤ PSLV has successfully launched landmark planetary
missions including Chandrayaan-1 (2008) and the
Mars Orbiter Mission (Mangalyaan, 2013).
➤ In February 2017, the PSLV-C37 mission estab-
lished a world record at the time by placing 104 satel-
lites into orbit in a single launch.
➤ Commercial launches using the PSLV are managed
and marketed globally by ISRO's commercial arm,
NewSpace India Limited (NSIL).

line.

➤ A Drive is a fast, flat, horizontal shot that travels
straight and close above the net.

sharply downwards with speed.
➤ The standard height of a badminton net is 1.55 me-
tres (5 feet 1 inch) at the edges and 1.524 metres (5
feet) at the center.

27.question_text_en: Teejan Bai is associated with which folk tradition?
27.question_text_hi: Teejan Bai is associated with which folk tradition?
27.explanation_en:
Teejan Bai is an internationally acclaimed exponent of
Pandavani, the traditional narrative folk singing art
form of Chhattisgarh.
Important Facts:
➤ In Pandavani, stories from the epic Mahabharata
are narrated with musical accompaniment, primarily
holding a stringed instrument called Tambura.
➤ Teejan Bai performs the Kapalik style of Pandavani,
characterized by dynamic enactments, while Vedamati
is the seated recitation style.
➤ She was honoured with the Padma Shri in 1988,
the Padma Bhushan in 2003, and the Padma
Vibhushan in 2019.
➤ She received the Sangeet Natak Akademi
Award in 1995 and the prestigious Fukuoka Arts
and Culture Prize in 2018.
➤ Pandavani is native to Chhattisgarh and neighbor-
ing tribal belts of Central India.

Pandavani belongs to which category of Indian
music?

Pandavani belongs to which category of Indian
music?
28.explanation_en:
Pandavani is categorized as a traditional folk musical
and storytelling art form originating from Chhattisgarh.
Important Facts:
➤ Folk music encompasses traditional regional perform-
ing art forms passed down orally across generations.
➤ In Pandavani, the lead artist enacts the heroic deeds
of the Pandavas, portraying Bhima as the central
heroic figure.
➤ The lead narrator is accompanied by supporting mu-
sicians playing instruments such as the Kartal,
Harmonium, and Dholak.
➤ The two prominent styles of Pandavani recitation are
the Vedamati style and the Kapalik style.
➤ Jhaduram Devangan, Punaram Nishad, and Teejan
Bai are the most renowned pioneers of this folk art.

29.question_text_en:
In Indo-Islamic architecture, what is the specific term
used for the open courtyard of a mosque?
29.question_text_hi:
In Indo-Islamic architecture, what is the specific term
used for the open courtyard of a mosque?
29.explanation_en:
In mosque architecture, the open central courtyard sur-
rounded by colonnades or arcades is called the Sahn.
Important Facts:
➤ The Sahn typically contains a central ablution foun-
tain or pool (Hauz) for performing ritual cleansing
(Wudu) before prayer.
➤ The Mihrab is a semicircular niche in the wall of a
mosque that indicates the direction of Mecca.
➤ Qibla refers to the exact direction toward the Kaaba
in Mecca, which Muslims face during daily prayers.
➤ The Liwan refers to the covered prayer hall or
colonnaded porch surrounding the open courtyard.
➤ The Minbar is the elevated pulpit from where the
Imam delivers the sermon (Khutbah).

30.question_text_en:
Which sage of ancient India authored the text known
as the Mimamsa-sutras?
30.question_text_hi:
Which sage of ancient India authored the text known
as the Mimamsa-sutras?
30.explanation_en:
Sage Jaimini, a disciple of sage Veda Vyasa, authored
the Mimamsa-sutras, which form the foundational
text of the Purva Mimamsa school of Hindu philosophy.
Important Facts:
➤ The Mimamsa-sutras emphasize the ritualistic in-
terpretation and authority of the Vedas, especially the
Samhitas and Brahmanas.
➤ Sage Badarayana authored the Brahma-sutras
(also called Vedanta-sutras), laying the foundation for
Uttara Mimamsa.
➤ Sage Charaka is renowned for compiling the foun-
dational medical treatise Charaka Samhita.
➤ Panini authored the famous Sanskrit grammatical
treatise Ashtadhyayi.
➤ The six orthodox schools of Hindu philosophy
(Shad-Darshana) include Nyaya, Vaisheshika,
Samkhya, Yoga, Mimamsa, and Vedanta.

31.question_text_en:
The 'Pancha Pandava Rathas' at Mahabalipuram are
an example of:
31.question_text_hi:
The 'Pancha Pandava Rathas' at Mahabalipuram are
an example of:
31.explanation_en:
The Pancha Pandava Rathas at Mahabalipuram
(Mamallapuram) are monolithic rock-cut struc-
tures, each carved entirely out of a single large block of
granite.
Important Facts:
➤ The Rathas were carved during the reign of Pallava
king Narasimhavarman I (Mamalla) in the 7th cen-
tury CE.
➤ The five monolithic shrines are named after the
Pandavas and Draupadi: Dharmaraja, Bhima, Arjuna,
Nakula-Sahadeva, and Draupadi.
➤ The largest and most elaborately carved ratha among
them is the Dharmaraja Ratha, dedicated to Lord
Shiva.
➤ Mahabalipuram is recognized globally as a
UNESCO World Heritage Site (inscribed in 1984).
➤ These temples represent the transition from rock-cut

cave temples to free-standing Dravidian structural
architecture.

32.question_text_en:
The Battle of Talikota (1565 AD) led to the decline of
which major South Indian empire?
32.question_text_hi:
The Battle of Talikota (1565 AD) led to the decline of
which major South Indian empire?
32.explanation_en:
The Battle of Talikota (also called the Battle of
Rakkasa-Tangadi) fought in 1565 AD brought a cata-
strophic defeat and led to the collapse of the
Vijayanagara Empire.
Important Facts:
➤ The battle was fought between the Vijayanagara
Empire led by de facto ruler Aliya Rama Raya and
the combined forces of the Deccan Sultanates (Bijapur,
Golconda, Ahmadnagar, and Bidar).
➤ Following the defeat, the magnificent capital city of

Hampi was comprehensively sacked and destroyed.
➤ The Vijayanagara Empire was founded in 1336 AD
by brothers Harihara I and Bukka Raya I of the
Sangama dynasty.
➤ After the battle, the capital was shifted southward to
Penukonda and later to Chandragiri under the
Aravidu dynasty.
➤ The prominent dynasties that ruled Vijayanagara
were Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva, and Aravidu.

33.question_text_en: What is meant by the opportunity cost?
33.question_text_hi: What is meant by the opportunity cost?
33.explanation_en:
In economics, opportunity cost represents the value
or benefit of the next best alternative foregone
when making a decision between mutually exclusive
choices.
Important Facts:
➤ The concept of opportunity cost is foundational to un-
derstanding the economic problem of scarcity and
choice.
➤ Austrian economist Friedrich von Wieser formu-
lated the formal concept of alternative or opportunity
cost.
➤ Opportunity cost includes both explicit out-of-pocket
expenses and implicit non-monetary trade-offs.
➤ The slope of the Production Possibility
Frontier (PPF) measures the marginal opportunity
cost of producing one good over another.
➤ Sunk costs (past non-recoverable expenditures) are
not considered when calculating opportunity cost.

34.question_text_en:
A "Deficit Budget" is usually preferred during which
economic condition?
34.question_text_hi:
A "Deficit Budget" is usually preferred during which
economic condition?
34.explanation_en:
A deficit budget—where government expenditures ex-
ceed revenues—is typically implemented during an eco-
nomic depression or recession to inject aggre-
gate demand and stimulate output and employment.
Important Facts:
➤ Deficit financing to pull an economy out of recession
is a central tenet of Keynesian economics, formu-
lated by John Maynard Keynes.
➤ In times of recession, increased government spend-
ing stimulates business investment and consumer pur-
chasing power through the fiscal multiplier effect.
➤ During periods of high inflation, governments
adopt a surplus budget or contractionary fiscal policy to
reduce excess demand.
➤ The main components of government budget deficits
include the fiscal deficit, revenue deficit, and pri-
mary deficit.
➤ In India, fiscal discipline targets are governed by the

Fiscal Responsibility and Budget
Management (FRBM) Act, 2003.

35.question_text_en:
Fill in the blank: The process of selling a portion of
the government's shareholding in a Public Sector
Undertaking (PSU) to private investors is called ________.
35.question_text_hi:
Fill in the blank: The process of selling a portion of
the government's shareholding in a Public Sector
Undertaking (PSU) to private investors is called ________.
35.explanation_en:
The process by which the government dilutes or sells its
equity stake in public sector enterprises to private in-
vestors is called Disinvestment.
Important Facts:
➤ Disinvestment can be minority disinvestment, major-
ity disinvestment, or complete strategic disinvest-
ment (privatization).
➤ In India, disinvestment policy gained major momen-
tum under the New Economic Policy of 1991.
➤ The Department of Investment and Public Asset
Management (DIPAM), under the Ministry of Finance,
manages the government's investments and disinvest-
ment in PSUs.
➤ Strategic disinvestment involves transferring a major
share of government equity along with the transfer of
management control.
➤ In 1999, a separate Department of Disinvestment
was established, which was renamed DIPAM in 2016.

36.question_text_en:
What does the term 'Financial Liberalization'
primarily refer to in the context of the 1991 reforms?
36.question_text_hi:
What does the term 'Financial Liberalization'
primarily refer to in the context of the 1991 reforms?
36.explanation_en:
In the 1991 economic reforms, financial liberalization pri-
marily meant deregulating financial markets and reduc-
ing private and foreign investment restric-
tions in banking and financial services.
Important Facts:
➤ Financial sector reforms in 1991 were initiated follow-
ing the recommendations of the Narasimham
Committee I (1991).
➤ The reforms reduced statutory reserve requirements
such as the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) and the
Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR).
➤ Interest rate structures were deregulated, allowing
commercial banks to determine deposit and lending
rates based on market forces.
➤ Private domestic banks and foreign banks were per-
mitted to establish operations and expand their presence
in India.
➤ The Securities and Exchange Board of India
(SEBI) was given statutory powers in 1992 to regulate
modern capital markets.

ing the recommendations of the Narasimham
Committee I (1991).
➤ The reforms reduced statutory reserve requirements
such as the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) and the
Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR).
➤ Interest rate structures were deregulated, allowing
commercial banks to determine deposit and lending
rates based on market forces.
➤ Private domestic banks and foreign banks were per-
mitted to establish operations and expand their presence
in India.
➤ The Securities and Exchange Board of India
(SEBI) was given statutory powers in 1992 to regulate
modern capital markets.

37.question_text_en: What does 'License Raj' refers to?
37.question_text_hi: What does 'License Raj' refers to?
37.explanation_en:
'License Raj' refers to the elaborate system of govern-
ment regulations, permits, and industrial licensing
required to set up and run businesses in India between
1947 and 1991.
Important Facts:
➤ The system was formalized through the Industries
(Development and Regulation) Act, 1951 and
the Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956.
➤ It created bureaucratic bottlenecks, red tape, and
quotas that severely restricted private enterprise growth.
➤ Under the License Raj, government approvals were
needed not just to set up a factory, but even to expand
output or introduce new products.
➤ The system was largely dismantled with the introduc-
tion of the New Industrial Policy on 24 July
1991.
➤ The 1991 policy abolished industrial licensing for all
except a handful of strategic, hazardous, and security-
related industries.

38.question_text_en:
Which Fundamental Right was removed by the 44th
Amendment?
38.question_text_hi:
Which Fundamental Right was removed by the 44th
Amendment?
38.explanation_en:
The Right to Property was removed from the list of
Fundamental Rights by the 44th Constitutional
Amendment Act, 1978.
Important Facts:
➤ Originally, the Right to Property was guaranteed as a
Fundamental Right under Article 19(1)(f) and
Article 31.
➤ Following the 44th Amendment, it was made a
legal/constitutional right under Article 300A in Part XII
of the Constitution.
➤ The 44th Amendment Act was enacted during the
tenure of the Morarji Desai-led Janata Party gov-
ernment.
➤ With this deletion, the total number of Fundamental
Rights in the Indian Constitution was reduced from
seven to six.
➤ Legal rights under Article 300A lack the direct remedy
under Article 32 of the Supreme Court's writ
jurisdiction.

39.question_text_en:
Which Article restricts discussion on the conduct of
Judges in Parliament?
39.question_text_hi:
Which Article restricts discussion on the conduct of
Judges in Parliament?
39.explanation_en:
Article 121 of the Constitution of India provides that
no discussion shall take place in Parliament regarding
the conduct of any Judge of the Supreme Court or High
Court in the discharge of their duties, except upon a mo-
tion for removal.
Important Facts:
➤ A corresponding provision, Article 211, prohibits
State Legislatures from discussing the conduct of
Supreme Court and High Court judges.
➤ Article 120 provides for the language to be used in
Parliament (Hindi or English).
➤ Article 122 states that courts cannot inquire into
the validity of proceedings of Parliament on grounds of
alleged irregularity of procedure.
➤ Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts can
only be removed under Article 124(4) on grounds of
proved misbehaviour or incapacity.
➤ The procedure for investigation and removal of
judges is regulated by the Judges (Inquiry) Act,
1968.

40.question_text_en: Who administers the oath to a Judge of a High Court?
40.question_text_hi: Who administers the oath to a Judge of a High Court?
40.explanation_en:
Under Article 219 of the Constitution of India, a Judge
of a High Court takes and subscribes an oath or affirma-
tion before the Governor of the State (or someone
appointed by them).
Important Facts:
➤ High Court judges are appointed by the President
of India under Article 217.
➤ The form of oath for High Court judges is prescribed
in the Third Schedule of the Constitution.
➤ A High Court judge can hold office until attaining the
age of 62 years.
➤ Under Article 217(1)(a), a High Court judge sub-
mits their resignation in writing addressed to the
President of India.
➤ Under Article 69, the Vice President takes oath be-
fore the President; under Article 159, the Governor
takes oath before the Chief Justice of the respective
High Court.

Conventions 138 and 182 in 2017.

42.question_text_en: Which layer of Earth is the thickest?
42.question_text_hi: Which layer of Earth is the thickest?
42.explanation_en:
The Mantle is the thickest layer of the Earth, extending
from the base of the crust down to a depth of approxi-
mately 2,900 km.
Important Facts:
➤ The mantle makes up about 84% of the Earth's total
volume and approximately 67% of its mass.
➤ The boundary separating the crust and the mantle is
known as the Mohorovičić discontinuity (Moho).
➤ The upper portion of the mantle, extending between
100 km and 400 km, is called the asthenosphere,
which is semi-fluid and drives tectonic plate movement.
➤ The boundary between the mantle and the outer core
is known as the Gutenberg discontinuity.
➤ The Earth's crust is the thinnest layer, with an aver-
age thickness of 5–30 km under oceanic and continental
plates.

43.question_text_en:
Which of the following cotton species is not cultivated
in India?
43.question_text_hi:
Which of the following cotton species is not cultivated
in India?
43.explanation_en:
Gossypium tomentosum is a wild, non-commercial
species of cotton endemic to the Hawaiian Islands and is
not cultivated in India.
Important Facts:
➤ India is the only country that grows all four commer-

cially cultivated species of cotton: *G. arboreum*, *G.
herbaceum*, *G. hirsutum*, and *G. barbadense*.
➤ *Gossypium arboreum* and *Gossypium herbaceum*
are diploid species known as Old World or Desi cot-
ton.
➤ *Gossypium hirsutum* (American cotton) and
*Gossypium barbadense* (Egyptian cotton) are
tetraploid New World species.
➤ *Gossypium hirsutum* accounts for the vast majority
of total cotton production in India.
➤ Cotton is primarily cultivated on nutrient-rich black
cotton soil (Regur soil), mainly in the Deccan
plateau.

44.question_text_en:
The wings of a butterfly and a bird are examples of
which structures?
44.question_text_hi:
The wings of a butterfly and a bird are examples of
which structures?
44.explanation_en:
The wings of a butterfly and a bird are analogous
structures because they perform the same function of
flight but have different embryonic origins and basic
anatomical structures.
Important Facts:
➤ Analogous structures arise as a result of conver-
gent evolution, where unrelated organisms adapt to
similar environments or ecological niches.
➤ Homologous structures share a common em-
bryonic origin and basic anatomy but perform different
functions (e.g., human arm and bat wing).
➤ Homologous organs are the result of divergent
evolution.
➤ Insect wings are non-cellular membranous folds sup-
ported by veins, whereas bird wings are modified fore-
limbs supported by bones.
➤ Vestigial organs are rudimentary structures that
have lost their ancestral function through evolution, such
as the human vermiform appendix.

options.text_en: Continuous view of the Sun without eclipses
options.text_hi: Continuous view of the Sun without eclipses

45.explanation_en:
The primary advantage of placing the Aditya-L1 satellite
in a halo orbit around the Sun-Earth Lagrange point 1
(L1) is having an uninterrupted, continuous view of
the Sun without any occultation or eclipses.
Important Facts:
➤ Aditya-L1 is India's first dedicated space mission to
study the Sun, developed and launched by ISRO.
➤ It was launched on 2 September 2023 aboard the
PSLV-C57 rocket from Sriharikota.
➤ The satellite successfully entered its halo orbit
around L1 on 6 January 2024.
➤ Lagrange Point 1 (L1) is located approximately 1.5
million kilometres away from Earth towards the Sun.
➤ The satellite carries seven scientific payloads to ob-
serve the photosphere, chromosphere, and solar corona.

46.question_text_en:
Why is a direct numerical comparison of the AQI
between India and the USA technically complex?
46.question_text_hi:
Why is a direct numerical comparison of the AQI
between India and the USA technically complex?
46.explanation_en:
A direct comparison is complex because the National Air
Quality Index of India and the US AQI use differing
category breakpoints and mathematical formulas
for converting pollutant concentrations into index values.
Important Facts:
➤ India's National AQI considers eight pollutants:
PM10, PM2.5, NO2, SO2, CO, O3, NH3, and Pb.
➤ The US EPA AQI monitors five major criteria pollu-
tants: ground-level ozone, PM (PM2.5 and PM10), CO,
SO2, and NO2.
➤ A concentration value of PM2.5 corresponds to differ-
ent AQI numbers and different health severity brackets
under Indian versus US standards.
➤ In India, the sub-index for PM2.5 is based on a 24-
hour average, with different thresholds for 'Good',
'Moderate', and 'Poor' categories.
➤ India's National AQI was launched in October
2014 by the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB).

28.question_text_en:
Avanaddha Vadya belongs to which category of
musical instruments?
28.question_text_hi:
Avanaddha Vadya belongs to which category of
musical instruments?
28.explanation_en:
In traditional Indian music classification from the Natya
Shastra, Avanaddha Vadya refers to membra-
nophones or percussion instruments where sound
is produced by striking a stretched animal hide or mem-
brane.
Important Facts:
➤ Bharata Muni's Natya Shastra categorizes Indian
instruments into four classes: Tata, Avanaddha, Ghana,
and Sushira.
➤ Tata Vadya comprises chordophones (stringed in-
struments like Veena, Sitar).
➤ Sushira Vadya represents aerophones (wind in-
struments like Bansuri, Shehnai).
➤ Ghana Vadya represents idiophones (solid instru-
ments without membranes like Manjira, Ghatam).
➤ Prominent examples of Avanaddha Vadya include
the Tabla, Mridangam, Dholak, and Pakhawaj.

30.question_text_en:

30.question_text_hi:
The Shigmo festival, a major spring celebration in
Goa and the Konkan region, is also known by which of the
following Sanskritized names?
30.explanation_en:
Shigmo (or Shigmotsav) is a vibrant spring festival cel-
ebrated in Goa, derived from the Sanskrit word
Shishirotsava, meaning the celebration marking the
end of winter (Shishir ritu).
Important Facts:
➤ Shigmo spans across the Hindu month of Phalguna
and is considered Goa's cultural equivalent of Holi.
➤ It features traditional street folk dances like Ghode
Modni, Fugdi, and Romtamel.
➤ The festival also celebrates the homecoming of war-
riors who had left at the end of Dussehra.
➤ Two distinct variants are celebrated: Dhakto
Shigmo (by rural farmers) and Vhadlo Shigmo
(larger urban celebrations).
➤ Saga Dawa and Losoong are
Buddhist/Himalayan festivals celebrated in Sikkim, not
the Konkan region.

Sanya, China in April 2011.

Yekaterinburg, Russia in June 2009.

African continent to the bloc.
➤ The 2014 Fortaleza Summit led to the establishment
of the New Development Bank (NDB).

➤ In 2024, BRICS further expanded to include coun-
tries like Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, and the UAE.

the Buddha and Bodhisatva figures specifically resemble
which Greek deity?
33.explanation_en:
Gandhara art is characterized by a Greco-Buddhist
synthesis where Buddha and Bodhisattva figures feature
wavy hair, sharp facial contours, and drapery modeled
heavily after the Greek god Apollo.
Important Facts:
➤ The Gandhara school flourished under the patronage
of the Kushana dynasty, especially Emperor
Kanishka.
➤ It prominently used grey schist stone and stucco to
sculpt sculptures.
➤ Major centers of this art included Taxila,
Peshawar, and Bagram.
➤ Buddha was depicted wearing heavy Roman-style
toga drapery with realistic anatomical precision.
➤ In contrast, the indigenous Mathura school of
art utilized spotted red sandstone.

36.question_text_en: What does elasticity of demand measures?
36.question_text_hi: What does elasticity of demand measures?

options.text_en: Responsiveness of demand to price changes
options.text_hi: Responsiveness of demand to price changes

36.explanation_en:
Elasticity of demand (specifically price elasticity)
measures the responsiveness or sensitivity of
the quantity demanded of a good to a change in its
price.
Important Facts:
➤ It is calculated as the percentage change in
quantity demanded divided by the percentage
change in price.
➤ When elasticity is greater than 1, demand is termed
elastic; when less than 1, it is inelastic.
➤ If demand does not change at all with price, it is
called perfectly inelastic ($E_d = 0$).
➤ If quantity drops to zero with any price rise, it is called
perfectly elastic ($E_d = \infty$).
➤ The concept was popularized and formalized in eco-
nomics by Alfred Marshall.

37.question_text_en:
What is the status of the concept of res gestae
(relevancy of facts forming part of the same transaction)
under the new Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam?
37.question_text_hi:
What is the status of the concept of res gestae
(relevancy of facts forming part of the same transaction)
under the new Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam?

options.text_en: Continues with similar principles as earlier law
options.text_hi: Continues with similar principles as earlier law

37.explanation_en:
The legal doctrine of res gestae (facts connected to
form part of the same transaction) has been retained un-
der Section 4 of the Bharatiya Sakshya
Adhiniyam, 2023, preserving the exact core princi-
ples previously contained in Section 6 of the Indian
Evidence Act, 1872.
Important Facts:
➤ Under the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, the doctrine
was codified under Section 6.
➤ Under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam
(BSA), 2023, it is placed in Section 4.
➤ It provides that facts which form part of the same
transaction are relevant, whether they occurred at the
same time and place or at different times and places.
➤ The BSA came into force on 1 July 2024, replacing
the colonial Indian Evidence Act.

➤ Res gestae serves as a well-established exception to
the general exclusion of hearsay evidence.

38.question_text_en:
What is the status of burden of proof under Bharatiya
Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA)?
38.question_text_hi:
What is the status of burden of proof under Bharatiya
Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA)?

options.text_en: It applies only in civil cases.
options.text_hi: It applies only in civil cases.

options.text_en: It is always on the accused.
options.text_hi: It is always on the accused.

options.text_en:
It primarily lies on the prosecution but may shift in specific
circumstances.
options.text_hi:
It primarily lies on the prosecution but may shift in specific
circumstances.

38.explanation_en:
Under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, the initial bur-
den of proving guilt rests fundamentally on the prose-
cution beyond reasonable doubt, but the onus can
shift to the accused in specific legal circumstances
(such as special knowledge or statutory presumptions).
Important Facts:
➤ The concept of burden of proof is covered under
Part III (Chapter VIII) of the Bharatiya Sakshya
Adhiniyam, 2023.
➤ Section 104 of the BSA provides that whoever de-
sires any court to give judgment dependent on legal
rights must prove facts.
➤ When an accused relies on general exceptions of the
law, the burden of proving their existence lies on the ac-
cused.
➤ The burden of proving fact especially within the
knowledge of any person lies upon that person.
➤ The BSA replaces the Indian Evidence Act, 1872
while retaining modern evidentiary standards.

39.question_text_en: Earth's axis is tilted at:
39.question_text_hi: Earth's axis is tilted at:
39.explanation_en:
Earth's rotational axis is tilted at an angle of approxi-
mately 23.4° (often rounded to 23.5°) relative to the
perpendicular to its orbital plane around the Sun.
Important Facts:
➤ This axial tilt is scientifically termed the Earth's
obliquity.
➤ The tilt relative to the plane of the ecliptic itself is
66.6° (or 66.5°).
➤ Earth's axial tilt is the primary cause of the cycle of
seasons on Earth.
➤ The Tropic of Cancer is located at approximately
23.5° N latitude.
➤ The Tropic of Capricorn is located at approxi-
mately 23.5° S latitude.

continental shelf, is India's largest domestic crude oil
producer.

Krishna-Godavari (KG) basin off the east coast.

41.question_text_en:
Fill in the blank: ______ part of the brain is
responsible for maintaining body posture and balance.
41.question_text_hi:
Fill in the blank: ______ part of the brain is
responsible for maintaining body posture and balance.
41.explanation_en:
The cerebellum, situated at the back of the brain
within the hindbrain, coordinates voluntary movements
and maintains posture, equilibrium, and bodily
balance.
Important Facts:
➤ The cerebellum is often referred to as the "little
brain".
➤ It receives information from the sensory systems,
spinal cord, and other parts of the brain to regulate mo-
tor movements.
➤ The medulla oblongata controls involuntary auto-

nomic functions like heartbeat, respiration, and blood
pressure.
➤ The cerebrum (part of the forebrain) is responsible
for higher thinking, memory, emotion, and perception.
➤ Impairment of the cerebellum can lead to ataxia,
characterized by a loss of coordination.

43.question_text_en:
What is the significance of Lagrange points in space
missions?
43.question_text_hi:
What is the significance of Lagrange points in space
missions?

options.text_en: They reduce fuel needs for stable positioning
options.text_hi: They reduce fuel needs for stable positioning

43.explanation_en:
Lagrange points are positions in space where the
gravitational forces of two large bodies balance the cen-
tripetal force required for a smaller object to move with
them, thereby drastically reducing the fuel
needed to maintain a stable position.
Important Facts:
➤ There are five Lagrange points (labeled L1
through L5) for any system of two orbiting bodies.
➤ India's Aditya-L1 solar observatory is placed in a
halo orbit around the Sun-Earth L1 point.
➤ Points L1, L2, and L3 lie on the line connecting the
two masses and are points of unstable equilibrium.
➤ The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST)
operates around the Sun-Earth L2 point.
➤ Points L4 and L5 form equilateral triangles with the
two large masses and are stable positions.

44.question_text_en:
How is the final numerical value of India's National
AQI (NAQI) determined for a 24-hour period?
44.question_text_hi:
How is the final numerical value of India's National
AQI (NAQI) determined for a 24-hour period?

options.text_en: Sum of the top three sub-indices
options.text_hi: Sum of the top three sub-indices

44.explanation_en:
Under India's National Air Quality Index (NAQI) method-
ology, the overall AQI value for a given location is deter-
mined by the maximum (highest) sub-index
value among all evaluated criteria pollutants.
Important Facts:
➤ The NAQI monitors 8 key pollutants: $PM_{10}$,
$PM_{2.5}$, $NO_2$, $SO_2$, $CO$, $O_3$, $NH_3$,
and $Pb$.
➤ A minimum of three pollutants must be monitored, of
which one must be $PM_{10}$ or $PM_{2.5}$, to calcu-
late the AQI.
➤ The dominant pollutant responsible for the highest
sub-index is designated as the lead pollutant.
➤ The index classifies air quality into 6 distinct cate-
gories: Good, Satisfactory, Moderately Polluted, Poor,
Very Poor, and Severe.
➤ NAQI was launched in India in October 2014 un-
der the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan.

"biological orphan", bereft (D) the social structures and
environmental cues it once thrived upon. A mammoth born
to a surrogate elephant mother would lack the ancestral
knowledge of migration patterns and social hierarchies. It
would be a creature displaced in time, existing as a lonely
curiosity rather than a functional member of a biological
community.
Ultimately, the question is not whether we possess the
genetic tools to reach into the past, but whether we ought
to proceed. Just because a scientific "could" exists doesn't
(E) a moral "should" follows. We must decide if our role is
to be the restorers of the past or the responsible guardians
of the present.

given alternatives.

Statehood Day, as Nagaland became the 16th state
of India on 1 December 1963.

30.question_text_en:
In which architectural tradition is the decorative
technique of Pietra Dura mainly employed?
30.question_text_hi:
In which architectural tradition is the decorative
technique of Pietra Dura mainly employed?
30.explanation_en:
Pietra Dura (Parchin Kari) is an inlay technique where
cut and fitted, highly polished semi-precious stones are
set into stone walls, prominently used in Mughal
tombs and monuments.
Important Facts:
➤ Pietra Dura reached its artistic pinnacle in India dur-
ing the reign of Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan.
➤ The technique is extensively displayed in world-fa-
mous monuments such as the Taj Mahal in Agra and
the Red Fort in Delhi.
➤ The tomb of Itimad-ud-Daulah in Agra is cele-
brated as one of the earliest Mughal structures to exten-
sively utilize Pietra Dura on white marble.
➤ The stones commonly inlaid include lapis lazuli, onyx,
jasper, turquoise, and carnelian.
➤ The technique originated in Italy during the 16th-cen-
tury Renaissance before being embraced and perfected
by Mughal artisans.

31.question_text_en:
In which type of economic system do the government
and the market together answer the questions of what to
produce, how to produce, and how to distribute?
31.question_text_hi:
In which type of economic system do the government
and the market together answer the questions of what to
produce, how to produce, and how to distribute?
31.explanation_en:
In a mixed economy, economic decisions concerning
production and distribution are answered jointly through
both the market price mechanism and govern-
ment planning.
Important Facts:
➤ India adopted a mixed economic system after
independence, balancing public sector control with pri-
vate enterprise.
➤ In a pure capitalist economy, decisions are
driven entirely by market forces of demand and supply
with minimal government intervention.
➤ In a pure socialist (command) economy, the
central government makes all decisions regarding pro-
duction, allocation, and pricing.
➤ The concept of a mixed economy gained prominence
in the 20th century, influenced by John Maynard Keynes.
➤ Under India's Industrial Policy Resolution of 1948
and 1956, key strategic sectors were reserved for the
public sector alongside private business.

32.question_text_en:
Under financial sector reforms 1991, the limit for
foreign investment in private sector banks is:
32.question_text_hi:
Under financial sector reforms 1991, the limit for
foreign investment in private sector banks is:
32.explanation_en:
Following financial sector liberalization initiated in 1991
and subsequent policy revisions, the composite ceiling
for foreign investment (FDI and FPI) in Indian private
sector banks was raised to 74 per cent.
Important Facts:
➤ Foreign investment up to 49 per cent in private
sector banks is permitted under the automatic route.
➤ Foreign investment beyond 49 per cent and up to 74
per cent is allowed under the government ap-
proval route.
➤ Financial sector reforms in India were initiated based
on the recommendations of the Narasimham
Committee I (1991).
➤ In public sector banks (PSBs), foreign investment is
capped at 20 per cent through the government ap-
proval route.
➤ Foreign investment rules ensure that at least 26 per
cent of paid-up capital in private banks remains under
resident Indian shareholding.

33.question_text_en:
Which Article abolishes titles except military and
academic distinctions, preventing creation of hereditary
privileges and ensuring equality among citizens?
33.question_text_hi:
Which Article abolishes titles except military and
academic distinctions, preventing creation of hereditary
privileges and ensuring equality among citizens?
33.explanation_en:
Article 18 of the Indian Constitution abolishes all titles,
explicitly barring the State from conferring titles on any-
one, except for military and academic distinctions, to en-
sure democratic equality.
Important Facts:
➤ Article 18(1) prohibits the State from conferring
any title except military or academic distinctions.
➤ Article 18(2) prohibits citizens of India from ac-
cepting any title from any foreign State.
➤ Article 17 provides for the abolition of "untouchabil-
ity" and forbids its practice in any form.
➤ The Supreme Court in the Balaji Raghavan case
(1996) upheld the validity of National Awards (Bharat
Ratna, Padma awards), ruling they are decorations and
not titles.
➤ National awards cannot be used as prefixes or suf-
fixes to the names of the awardees.

34.question_text_en:
Which feature of Indian Constitution best reflects
principle of cooperative federalism through institutional
mechanisms enabling collaboration between Union and
states in policy formulation?
34.question_text_hi:
Which feature of Indian Constitution best reflects
principle of cooperative federalism through institutional
mechanisms enabling collaboration between Union and
states in policy formulation?
34.explanation_en:
The Inter-State Council, established under Article
263, serves as a dedicated constitutional institutional
mechanism fostering coordination, consultation, and co-
operative federalism between the Union and states.
Important Facts:
➤ Article 263 empowers the President to establish
an Inter-State Council to inquire into and advise upon
disputes and common policy issues.
➤ It was first established in 1990 following recommen-
dations of the Sarkaria Commission (1988).
➤ The Prime Minister acts as the Chairman of the
Inter-State Council.
➤ Its members include Chief Ministers of all States,
Chief Ministers/Administrators of Union Territories, and
six Union Cabinet Ministers.
➤ Unlike emergency provisions which centralize power,
the Inter-State Council promotes decentralized consen-
sus-building.

35.question_text_en:
Which situation best demonstrates legislative flexibility
of Indian federalism allowing Parliament to legislate on
State List temporarily?
35.question_text_hi:
Which situation best demonstrates legislative flexibility
of Indian federalism allowing Parliament to legislate on
State List temporarily?
35.explanation_en:
Under Article 250, during the operation of a
National Emergency (proclaimed under Article 352),
the Parliament acquires the power to make laws for the
whole or any part of India on matters enumerated in the
State List.
Important Facts:
➤ Article 352 empowers the President to proclaim a
National Emergency on grounds of war, external aggres-
sion, or armed rebellion.
➤ During a National Emergency, under Article 250,
Parliament gains overriding power to legislate on any
subject in the State List.
➤ Laws made by Parliament under Article 250 cease to
have effect six months after the proclamation of emer-
gency ceases to operate.
➤ Additionally, under Article 249, the Rajya Sabha
can authorize Parliament to legislate on a State List sub-
ject in the national interest by a two-thirds majority.
➤ This unitary shift during extraordinary situations illus-
trates the organic flexibility of Indian federalism.

36.question_text_en:
Article 134 relates to appeals to the Supreme Court in
which matters?
36.question_text_hi:
Article 134 relates to appeals to the Supreme Court in
which matters?
36.explanation_en:
Article 134 of the Indian Constitution provides for the
appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in
regard to criminal matters.
Important Facts:
➤ Under Article 134, an appeal lies to the Supreme
Court against judgments in criminal proceedings of a
High Court under specific conditions.
➤ If a High Court reverses an acquittal and sentences
an accused person to death, an appeal lies as of right.
➤ In contrast, appeals in civil matters to the
Supreme Court are governed by Article 133.
➤ Article 132 provides appellate jurisdiction in certain
cases involving constitutional interpretation.
➤ Article 136 provides discretionary power to grant
Special Leave to Appeal (SLP).

37.question_text_en:
Why do polar regions experience extreme daylight or
darkness for extended periods during certain times of the
year?
37.question_text_hi:
Why do polar regions experience extreme daylight or
darkness for extended periods during certain times of the
year?
37.explanation_en:
The extreme periods of daylight and darkness in polar
regions occur due to Earth's axial tilt effect
($23.5^\circ$) relative to its orbital plane as it revolves
around the Sun.
Important Facts:
➤ Earth's rotational axis is tilted at an angle of
$23.5^\circ$ from the perpendicular to its orbital plane
(or $66.5^\circ$ to the plane).
➤ During the summer solstice in June, the North Pole
is tilted continuously toward the Sun, causing the phe-
nomenon of the Midnight Sun.
➤ Conversely, during this period, the South Pole is
tilted away from the Sun, remaining in continuous dark-
ness (polar night).
➤ The boundary lines marking continuous 24-hour day
or night are the Arctic Circle ($66.5^\circ\text{ N}$)
and Antarctic Circle ($66.5^\circ\text{ S}$).
➤ Axial tilt combined with Earth's revolution is also the
primary driver for the cycle of seasons on Earth.

Gordon" theory or the concept of "Isostasy" in
Geomorphology?
38.question_text_hi:
Which of the following best describes the "Ogilvie-
Gordon" theory or the concept of "Isostasy" in
Geomorphology?

38.explanation_en:
Isostasy refers to the state of gravitational equi-
librium between Earth's lithosphere (crust) and as-
thenosphere (mantle), wherein tectonic blocks float at an
elevation proportional to their crustal thickness and den-
sity.
Important Facts:
➤ The term isostasy was proposed in 1889 by
American geologist Clarence Dutton.
➤ The concept is explained primarily through two classi-
cal models: the Airy hypothesis (constant density,
varying depth of roots) and the Pratt hypothesis
(varying density, uniform depth of compensation).
➤ Maria Ogilvie Gordon was a pioneering geologist
known for her groundbreaking tectonics and structural
geomorphology work in the Dolomites.
➤ Continental crust has a lower average density
($\approx 2.7\text{ g/cm}^3$) compared to oceanic crust
($\approx 3.0\text{ g/cm}^3$) and the mantle ($\approx
3.3\text{ g/cm}^3$).
➤ Isostatic rebound occurs when heavy surface loads
(such as massive ice sheets) melt, causing the de-
pressed crust to slowly rise.

39.explanation_en:
While thermohaline circulation is physically driven by
density variations from temperature and salinity, ocean-
wide circulation and deep mixing receive significant ki-
netic driving energy from tidal dissipation caused by the
gravitational pull of the moon and sun.
Important Facts:
➤ The word thermohaline derives from *thermo-*
(temperature) and *haline* (salinity), which govern sea-
water density.
➤ Tidal energy generated by the gravitational pull
of the moon and sun provides critical mechanical
energy required for deep-ocean vertical mixing.
➤ Cold, salty water sinks in polar regions such as the
North Atlantic and spreads through the deep ocean
basins.
➤ This global overturning conveyor belt plays a pivotal
role in regulating Earth's climate by redistributing heat
across latitudes.
➤ The complete global overturn cycle takes approxi-
mately 1,000 years to traverse.

40.question_text_en:
What is the largest part of the northern plain, which is
formed of older alluvium, called?
40.question_text_hi:
What is the largest part of the northern plain, which is
formed of older alluvium, called?
40.explanation_en:
The largest part of the northern plains is composed of
older alluvial soil and is called Bhangar. It lies above
the floodplains of the rivers and presents a terrace-like
feature.
Important Facts:
➤ Bhangar contains calcareous deposits locally
known as kankar.
➤ Khadar refers to the newer, younger alluvial de-
posits of the floodplains that are renewed almost every
year.
➤ Bhabar is a narrow belt (8 to 16 km wide) along the
foothills of the Shiwaliks composed of pebbles where
streams disappear.
➤ Terai is a wet, swampy, and marshy tract lying south
of the Bhabar belt with thick forest cover.
➤ Alluvial soil is the most widespread soil type in India,
covering around 40% of the country's total land area.

41.question_text_en:

matched with its cropping season in Northern States?
41.question_text_hi:
Which of the following pairs of crops is correctly
matched with its cropping season in Northern States?
41.explanation_en:
Zaid is the short summer cropping season between
Rabi and Kharif (from March to June) during which crops

and cucumber are cultivated.

Rabi, and Zaid.

clude rice, maize, cotton, and jowar.

ples include wheat, gram, barley, and mustard.
➤ Wheat, gram, and mustard are typical Rabi crops,
making options (a), (b), and (d) incorrectly matched.
➤ Zaid crops rely heavily on artificial irrigation during
the dry summer months before the southwest monsoon
arrives.

42.question_text_en:
Which fundamental force of nature is responsible for
keeping planets, including Earth, in stable orbits around
the Sun in the solar system?
42.question_text_hi:
Which fundamental force of nature is responsible for
keeping planets, including Earth, in stable orbits around
the Sun in the solar system?
42.explanation_en:
Gravitational attraction is the fundamental force
that binds celestial bodies together and provides the
necessary centripetal force to keep planets in stable or-
bits around the Sun.
Important Facts:
➤ Gravitational force is mathematically described by
Sir Isaac Newton's Law of Universal
Gravitation (1687).
➤ It is formulated as $F = G \frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}$,
where $G$ is the universal gravitational constant
($6.674 \times 10^{-11} \text{
N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{kg}^2$).
➤ Gravity is the weakest of the four fundamental forces
of nature, but it operates over infinite distances.
➤ In Albert Einstein's General Theory of
Relativity (1915), gravity is described as the curvature
of spacetime caused by mass and energy.
➤ Gravity governs orbital dynamics, tides on Earth, and
large-scale cosmic structure formation.

43.question_text_en:
The muscular tube that connects the kidney to the
urinary bladder is called:
43.question_text_hi:
The muscular tube that connects the kidney to the
urinary bladder is called:
43.explanation_en:
The ureter is the muscular tube that transports urine
from the renal pelvis of each kidney to the urinary
bladder through peristaltic contractions.
Important Facts:
➤ The human body has two ureters, one originating
from each kidney, measuring about 25 to 30 cm in length
in adults.
➤ Urine is propelled downward along the ureter into the
bladder by waves of smooth muscle contraction called
peristalsis.
➤ The urethra is the tube that conveys urine from the
urinary bladder to the outside of the body during urina-
tion.
➤ The nephron is the structural and functional micro-
scopic filtration unit of the kidney.
➤ The renal artery carries oxygenated, unfiltered
blood from the abdominal aorta directly to the kidney.

early diagnosis and effective treatment of diseases in
healthcare systems?

ing, automated laboratory analyzers, and genomic test-
ing, fundamentally improve diagnosis accuracy
and enable targeted therapies.
Important Facts:

scans, and PET scans allow high-resolution visual-
ization of internal organs.
➤ Molecular diagnostics such as PCR and next-gener-
ation sequencing allow detection of pathogens and ge-
netic anomalies at early stages.
➤ Precision medicine uses targeted diagnostic data to
select customized therapeutic treatments for patients.
➤ Robotic-assisted surgery and telemedicine improve
treatment outcomes and expand specialist healthcare
reach.
➤ Early and accurate diagnosis significantly lowers pa-
tient mortality rates and overall disease burden.

26.explanation_en:
Under official Badminton World Federation (BWF) rules,
the server delivers the service from the right service
court when their score is even (or zero).
Important Facts:
➤ When the server's score is odd (1, 3, 5, etc.), the
service is delivered from the left service court.
➤ The receiver must stand diagonally opposite to the
server in the corresponding service court.
➤ In modern badminton, the rally point scoring
system is followed, where a match is played as the
best of 3 games of 21 points each.
➤ A service court error occurs if a player serves or re-
ceives out of turn or from the incorrect service court.
➤ The global governing body for the sport is the
Badminton World Federation (BWF), headquar-
tered in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia.

27.explanation_en:
The Wangala festival, also known as the 100
Drums Festival, is the most important post-harvest

festival of the Garo tribe in Meghalaya.
Important Facts:
➤ Wangala is celebrated in honor of Saljong (the Sun
God of fertility), marking the end of the agricultural sow-
ing season.
➤ It is popularly known as the 100 Drums Festival
because men beat long cylindrical nagra drums in uni-
son.
➤ The rhythmic community dance is performed with
women and men clad in traditional vibrant headgear
called Kotip.
➤ The Garo Hills region in Meghalaya is the tradi-
tional homeland of the Garo (A.chik) community.
➤ Other notable traditional festivals of Meghalaya in-
clude the Nongkrem Dance and Shad Suk
Mynsiem celebrated by the Khasi tribe.

30.question_text_en:
In the Mathura school of art, what does the "Ushnisa"

30.question_text_hi:
In the Mathura school of art, what does the "Ushnisa"
on the Buddha's head represent?
30.explanation_en:
In the Mathura school of art, the Ushnisa is de-
picted as a cranial protuberance or fleshy bump on top
of the Buddha's head, symbolizing transcendent spiritual
wisdom.
Important Facts:
➤ Ushnisa is one of the 32 Mahapurusha
Lakshana (physical marks of a Great Being) associ-
ated with the Buddha.
➤ In early Mathura sculptures from the Kushana period,
it often appeared as a coiled spiral topknot resembling a
snail-shell or fleshy protuberance.
➤ The Mathura school of art flourished primarily
under the patronization of the Kushana Empire (1st
to 3rd century CE).
➤ Mathura art predominantly used spotted red sand-
stone sourced from Sikri and adjoining areas.
➤ Unlike Gandhara art which was Greco-Roman influ-
enced, the Mathura style developed an indigenous
Indian iconographic tradition.

➤ The Eighth Plan (1992–1997) targeted 5.6% and
achieved 6.68%.

before the Planning Commission was replaced by NITI
Aayog in 2015.

33.question_text_en:
Which constitutional provision ensures equality before
law and equal protection of laws, forming the basis of rule
of law and prohibiting arbitrary state action in governance?
33.question_text_hi:
Which constitutional provision ensures equality before
law and equal protection of laws, forming the basis of rule
of law and prohibiting arbitrary state action in governance?
33.explanation_en:
Article 14 of the Indian Constitution provides that the
State shall not deny to any person equality before
the law or the equal protection of the laws
within the territory of India.

Important Facts:
➤ The concept of 'Equality before Law' is of
British origin and forms an element of Dicey's Rule of
Law.
➤ The concept of 'Equal Protection of the Laws'
is borrowed from the American Constitution (14th
Amendment).
➤ Article 14 protects both citizens and non-citi-
zens (foreigners) as well as legal persons (corpora-
tions).
➤ The Supreme Court has ruled that the Rule of Law
embodied in Article 14 is a part of the basic structure
of the Constitution.
➤ Article 12 defines the term 'State', while Article 13
provides for judicial review of laws inconsistent with

33.explanation_hi:
Article 14 of the Indian Constitution provides that the
State shall not deny to any person equality before
the law or the equal protection of the laws
within the territory of India.

Important Facts:
➤ The concept of 'Equality before Law' is of
British origin and forms an element of Dicey's Rule of
Law.
➤ The concept of 'Equal Protection of the Laws'
is borrowed from the American Constitution (14th
Amendment).
➤ Article 14 protects both citizens and non-citi-
zens (foreigners) as well as legal persons (corpora-
tions).
➤ The Supreme Court has ruled that the Rule of Law
embodied in Article 14 is a part of the basic structure
of the Constitution.
➤ Article 12 defines the term 'State', while Article 13
provides for judicial review of laws inconsistent with
Fundamental Rights.

34.question_text_en:
Which Article abolishes untouchability and declares its
practice in any form as an offence punishable by law?
34.question_text_hi:
Which Article abolishes untouchability and declares its
practice in any form as an offence punishable by law?
34.explanation_en:
Article 17 of the Indian Constitution abolishes un-
touchability and forbids its practice in any form, mak-
ing its enforcement a punishable offence.
Important Facts:
➤ Article 17 is an absolute right that is available
against both the State and private individuals.
➤ The term 'untouchability' is not defined in the
Constitution or in any Act of Parliament.
➤ To enforce Article 17, Parliament enacted the
Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955, renamed in
1976 as the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955.
➤ Article 16 guarantees equality of opportunity in mat-
ters of public employment.
➤ Article 18 provides for the abolition of all titles, except
military and academic distinctions.
